title: Line-Conditioned Orthographic Organization in the Voynich Manuscript
summary: This preprint tests whether a previous word’s orthographic class improves prediction of the next class beyond section and relative line position. It reports positive gains across shifted folio-based partitions of one reconstructed transcription, while emphasizing incomplete source verification, exploratory model development, and the lack of independently confirmed physical line boundaries.
established: The reconstructed ZL3b working corpus contains 37,602 accepted tokens across 227 folio identifiers. Eighteen classes use word openings and length, and are operational spelling bins rather than grammatical categories (sections 2.1–2.2).

In three overlapping folio-grouped test partitions, development-tuned first-order models improve next-class log loss over section and line-position baselines by 0.0415, 0.0644 and 0.0413 nats per eligible token; folio bootstrap intervals exclude zero. Maximum gains in 30 position-matched random-predecessor placebos are lower in every split (sections 2.3 and 3.1–3.2).

A source audit checked 3,387 records containing 23,036 tokens against a PDF rendering; it did not establish complete byte-accurate reconstruction. A separate exclusion sensitivity retained positive gains but changed both the corpus and partitions, so its estimates are not paired with the originals (sections 3.6–3.7).

A position-aware selection and copying simulator did not recover the observed transition gain under the tested parameters, which were not jointly optimized for the relevant constraints; the authors do not rule out other copying mechanisms (sections 2.4 and 4).

open.question: Does the held-out next-class prediction gain persist using a byte-verified IVTFF import and independent transliterations?
open.check: Freeze the class definitions, folio-grouped splits and model-selection procedure, reconstruct the source from its original file, then compare the gain and position-matched predecessor controls across independent transcription witnesses.

open.question: Can the claimed change in predecessor prediction at line boundaries be confirmed for physical handwritten lines?
open.check: Blindly verify a prespecified sample of transcription line boundaries against high-resolution images and rerun the boundary comparison on verified cases.
